title: Dynamic Deterministic Constant-Approximate Distance Oracles with n^{ε} Worst-Case Update Time
authors: Bernhard Haeupler (University of Sofia "St. Kliment Ohridski" & ETH Zurich), Yaowei Long (University of Michigan), Thatchaphol Saranurak (University of Michigan)
abstract: We present a new distance oracle in the fully dynamic setting: given a weighted undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices undergoing both edge insertions and deletions, and an arbitrary parameter $\epsilon\in[1/\log^{c} n, 1]$ where $c>0$ is a small constant, we can deterministically maintain a data structure with $O(n^{\epsilon})$ worst-case update time that, given any pair of vertices $(u,v)$, returns a $2^{{\rm poly}(1/\epsilon)}$-approximate distance between $u$ and $v$ in ${\rm poly}(1/\epsilon)\log\log n$ query time. Our algorithm significantly advances the state-of-the-art in two aspects, both for fully dynamic algorithms and even decremental algorithms. First, no existing algorithm with worst-case update time guarantees a $o(n)$-approximation while also achieving an $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$ update and $n^{o(1)}$ query time, while our algorithm offers a constant $O_\eps(1)$-approximation with $O(n^\epsilon)$ update time and $O_{\epsilon}(\log \log n)$ query time. Second, even if amortized update time is allowed, it is the first deterministic constant-approximation algorithm with $n^{1-\Omega(1)}$ update and query time. The best result in this direction is the recent deterministic distance oracle by Chuzhoy and Zhang [STOC 2023] which achieves an approximation of $(\log\log n)^{2^{O(1/\epsilon^{3})}}$ with amortized update time of $O(n^{\epsilon})$ and query time of $2^{\rm poly}(1/\epsilon)}\log n\log\log n$. We obtain the result by dynamizing tools related to length-constrained expanders [Haeupler-Räcke-Ghaffari, STOC 2022; Haeupler-Hershkowitz-Tan, FOCS 2024]. Our technique completely bypasses the 40-year-old Even-Shiloach tree, which has remained the most pervasive tool in the area but is inherently amortized.

I. I NTRODUCTION
The dynamic distance oracle problem (or the dynamic allpairs shortest paths problem) is one of the most well-studied
dynamic graph problems since the beginning of the field. In
this problem, given an undirected weighted graph G = (V, E)
with n vertices undergoing edge insertions and deletions, the
goal is to build a data structure that given a vertex pair (u, v),
quickly returns an (approximate) distance between u and v.
The time required to update the data structure for each edge
update is called update time. The data structure has t worstcase update time if every update needs at most t time. On
the other hand, it has t amortized update time if it only
guarantees that after U updates for all large enough U , the
total time taken is at most t × U . The time to answer each
distance query is called query time. If the algorithms handle

The technique we use to prove Theorem 1 completely
bypasses the Even-Shiloach tree. Instead we dynamize tools
based on length-constrained expanders, which were recently
introduced by Haeupler, Räcke, and Ghaffari [3]. At a high
level, length-constrained expanders are a generalization of
expanders that offer the same advantages (e.g., robustness
under updates, low congestion routing) but in addition to
approximating flows and cuts also provide approximations
and control over distances. Thanks to the recent expansion
of this theory to constant-step expanders [4], [5] and efficient
algorithms for them [4] constant-step length-constrained expanders can even achieve constant-fractor approximations and
go beyond the polylogarithmic flow-cut gap inherent in regular
expanders and their decompositions.
Now, we highlight our novel technical components, which
may be of independent interest, by placing them in the
context of previous works. A high-level discussion on how we
construct and use these components can be found in Section II.
Before going into details, we first introduce the online-batch
dynamic setting. Unlike the fully dynamic setting in which we
receive a sequence of updates, in the online-batch dynamic
setting, the updates come in the form of several online batches.
The algorithm needs to handle the batches one by one, and
the update time for each batch should be roughly proportional
(with a small overhead, e.g. n ) to the size of this batch in
the worst case.4 A standard reduction to obtain fully dynamic
algorithms (with worst-case update time) from online-batch
algorithms was explicitly shown in [26], [34]. Therefore, we
will aim at online-batch dynamic distance oracles and most
components introduced below are online-batch dynamic.

b) Deamortization.: Deamortization is another major research program in dynamic algorithms (e.g. [24]–[27]) since
worst-case update time guarantees are required by many realworld applications and also some reductions [28]. For dynamic
distance oracles, the deamortization challenge highlights one
of the biggest gap of our understanding. While decremental
(2k − 1)-approximation algorithms with n1/k+o(1) amortized
update time and O(log log n) query time are known [8], [29],
there is no non-trivial algorithm with n2−Ω(1) worst-case
update time and no(1) query time!
There are two explanations behind the lack of progress.
First, a conditional lower bound [30, Corollary 5.10] implies that, any decremental or incremental distance oracle
with (5/3 − )-approximation cannot have n2−Ω(1) worst-case
update time and no(1) query time. However, this does not
explain the lack of progress in larger approximation regimes.
The deeper explanation is that all known fully dynamic and
decremental algorithms with n2−Ω(1) update time and no(1)
query time share one common technique that is inherently
amortized, called the Even-Shiloach tree [31], [32].3 This
technique is already 40 year old, yet no alternative techniques
were developed to avoid amortization until now.
Is there a fully dynamic (or even decremental) distance
oracle with o(n)-approximation, n2−Ω(1) worst-case update
time, and no(1) query time? More specifically, can we avoid
the Even-Shioach tree?

a) Multicommodity Maxflow with Unit Vertex Capacity.:
In the maximum multicommodity flow problem with unit

In this overview, for simplicity, we assume that all input graphs have constant degree. Moreover, we consider the
online-batch dynamic setting, in which a dynamic algorithm
only needs to handle a constant number of batched updates
π (1) , π (2) , ..., π (t) , instead of a long sequence of unit updates.
The update time to handle π (i) should be |π (i) | · nO() in
the worst case. Then, a standard reduction can transform an
online-batch dynamic algorithm to a fully dynamic algorithm
with worst-case update time.
For better understanding, we want to clarify the difference
between online-batch dynamic algorithms and fully dynamic
algorithms with amortized update time. The former is stronger
than the latter in the sense that an online-batch dynamic
algorithm can be transformed into a fully dynamic algorithm

not work in the online-batch dynamic setting. Precisely, for a

III. C ONCLUSIONS AND O PEN P ROBLEMS
In this paper, we design the first dynamic deterministic constant-approximate distance oracles with n worst-case
update time, and along the way, we develop a few algorithmic tools that may be of independent interest, including local length-constrained flows, dynamic routers, dynamic
length-constrained expander decompositions, dynamic lengthreducing emulators and dynamic vertex sparsifiers for distances.
Below, we list a few interesting open problems.
1) Optimal approximation-time trade-off: Our approximation ratio of O(exp(poly(1/))) seems far from being
optimal. For example, the decremental algorithm against
an oblivious adversary by Chechik [8] has (2 + )k −
1)-approximation with O(n1/k+o(1) ) amortized update
time. It is a challenging open problem to match this
trade-off with algorithms against an adaptive adversary,
even in the decremental and amortized setting. Getting
poly(1/)-approximation in n update time is already
very interesting.
2) Dynamic strong expander decomposition: We only
show how to maintain length-constrained expander decomposition in a weak sense. That is, as shown in
Theorem 3, we maintain a moving cut C such that
any reasonable demand in G − C can be routed in
the original graph G with small length and congestion,
while a strong decomposition requires that reasonable
demands in G − C can be routed in G − C. Can one
show a dynamic algorithm for maintaining strong lengthconstrained expander decomposition? In the non-lengthconstrained setting, a near-linear time weak expander
decomposition algorithm was also developed first [77]
and was later improved to strong expander decomposition [39].
3) Dynamic vertex sparsifier with worst-case update
time: Our dynamic vertex sparsifiers preserving distances with constant approximation (Theorem 6) have
amortized update time because the standard reduction
from the online-batch dynamic setting to the fully dynamic setting does not work directly when maintaining
an explicit object. Hence, it is still an open problem to
obtain a deterministic fully dynamic vertex sparsifier for
distances with constant approximation and n worst-case

Gutenberg [33] have shown dynamic vertex sparsifiers
preserving distances with worst-case update time, while
their sparsifiers have no(1) approximation and no(1)

4) Local length-constrained (1 + )-approximate maximum flow: As shown in Theorem 2, we localize the
approximate length-constrained maxflow algorithm by
Haeupler, Hershkowitz and Saranurak [42]. However,
our local algorithm only achieves (2 + )-approximation
instead of (1 + )-approximation as in [42]. The bottleneck is localizing the approximate lightest path blockers
algorithm, a key intermediate step in [42]. It will be
interesting to get a (1 + )-approximate local lengthconstrained maxflow algorithm.
